steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our DeepZero paper on scaling up zeroth-order optimization to train deep neural networks. Motivate why ZO optimization is needed where gradients are unavailable, compare it with BP-free alternatives, explain why it has not scaled so far, and list our main contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- FO gradient methods are the default for training, but not always usable
- ZO optimization as an alternative, and where it is needed
- Other BP-free methods vs. ZO
- Scalability bottleneck of ZO for DNN training
- Research question (Q), DeepZero and contributions
- Scope clarification

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- FO methods default
  - optimization algorithms crucial for training complex models, insights + predictive power across domains
  - FO gradient-based methods: SGD and variants (cite) default; use gradients to iteratively update params, minimize loss
  - but FO gradients sometimes unavailable or infeasible
- ZO optimization (cite)
  - finite differences of function values estimate gradients, no explicit gradients
  - minor modifications to FO algorithms
  - physics/chemistry: models interact with non-differentiable simulators/experiments (cite)
  - black-box learning with third-party APIs: adversarial attack and defense on black-box DL models (cite); black-box prompt learning for language-model-as-a-service (cite)
  - backpropagation (BP) (cite) may not be supported on hardware systems (cite)
- BP-free alternatives
  - biologically plausible: forward gradient methods (cite), greedy layer-wise learning (cite), Hebbian learning (cite)
  - need computational graphs, depend on DL frameworks / architectures
  - ZO only needs model queries -> broad applicability to black-box query-only problems
- Scalability bottleneck
  - hinders medium/large-scale DNN training (cite)
  - accuracy and efficiency degrade as dimension grows; ZO estimates biased, bias worse in high dimension (cite)
- (Q) How to scale up ZO optimization for training deep models? -> DeepZero: model pruning + parallel computing (Fig. 1)
  - CGE (deterministic coordinate-wise) beats RGE (randomized vector-wise) in accuracy and efficiency; more so as depth grows
  - sparsity crucial for CGE; obtained for 'free' by extending pruning-at-initialization to ZO; pruning + CGE synergy
  - parallelization-fit property of CGE -> forward parallelization; feature reuse removes redundant computation
  - experiments: image classification benchmarks + real-world black-box DL; ResNet20 on CIFAR-10 -> 86.94\% test accuracy, best for gradient-free training; black-box defense for adversarial robustness (cite), physics-informed DL with solver-in-the-loop (cite)
- Scope: extend ZO scalability where FO is hard/infeasible; not meant to solve scalability of training deep networks at any scale

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In machine learning (ML), optimization algorithms have played a crucial role in making it possible to train complex models, and this gave unprecedented insights and predictive capabilities in many different domains. Over the years, first-order (FO) gradient-based methods, like stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, became the default choice for training models. These methods use gradient information to update the model parameters iteratively, in order to minimize a given loss function. But there are several practical settings where FO gradient information is not available or is infeasible to compute, so other strategies are needed. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has come up as a promising approach for these challenges, because it uses finite differences of function values to estimate gradients, instead of asking for explicit gradient information. So with small modifications to FO algorithms, ZO optimization can be used in many real-world situations where FO gradients are hard to get. For example, in fields like physics and chemistry, ML models may interact with complicated simulators or experiments where the underlying systems are not differentiable. Also, black-box learning scenarios often come up when deep learning (DL) models are combined with third-party APIs, such as adversarial attack and defense against black-box DL models and black-box prompt learning for language-model-as-a-service. And the backpropagation (BP) mechanism for computing FO gradients may also not be supported when DL models are implemented on hardware systems. Besides ZO optimization, another related research direction in DL is about developing BP-free methods that are biologically plausible. Examples are forward gradient-based methods, greedy layer-wise learning, and Hebbian learning. But these techniques need access to computational graphs and depend a lot on the DL software frameworks and/or model architectures being used. ZO optimization on the other hand only relies on model queries and does not use computational graphs. So ZO optimization can be applied broadly to DL problems with black-box components that can only be queried. Even though ZO optimization is promising, scalability bottlenecks stop it from being used in medium or large-scale DNN training. When the problem dimension increases, traditional ZO methods get worse in accuracy and efficiency. The reason is that ZO gradient estimates based on finite differences are biased estimators of FO gradients, and the bias gets bigger in higher-dimensional spaces.

- (Q) How to scale up ZO optimization for training deep models? -> DeepZero (model pruning + parallel computing, Fig. 1). Contributions:
  - CGE vs RGE: CGE better accuracy and efficiency, more so with depth
  - sparsity crucial for CGE; free via pruning-at-initialization extended to ZO
  - parallelization-fit property -> forward parallelization, feature reuse
  - DeepZero experiments: ResNet20 on CIFAR-10, 86.94\% test accuracy (best gradient-free); black-box defense, physics-informed DL with solver-in-the-loop
- Scope: not meant to solve scalability of deep network training at any scale

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In machine learning (ML), optimization algorithms have played a crucial role in making it possible to train complex models, and this gave unprecedented insights and predictive capabilities in many different domains. Over the years, first-order (FO) gradient-based methods, like stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants, became the default choice for training models. These methods use gradient information to update the model parameters iteratively, in order to minimize a given loss function. But there are several practical settings where FO gradient information is not available or is infeasible to compute, so other strategies are needed. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has come up as a promising approach for these challenges, because it uses finite differences of function values to estimate gradients, instead of asking for explicit gradient information. So with small modifications to FO algorithms, ZO optimization can be used in many real-world situations where FO gradients are hard to get. For example, in fields like physics and chemistry, ML models may interact with complicated simulators or experiments where the underlying systems are not differentiable. Also, black-box learning scenarios often come up when deep learning (DL) models are combined with third-party APIs, such as adversarial attack and defense against black-box DL models and black-box prompt learning for language-model-as-a-service. And the backpropagation (BP) mechanism for computing FO gradients may also not be supported when DL models are implemented on hardware systems. Besides ZO optimization, another related research direction in DL is about developing BP-free methods that are biologically plausible. Examples are forward gradient-based methods, greedy layer-wise learning, and Hebbian learning. But these techniques need access to computational graphs and depend a lot on the DL software frameworks and/or model architectures being used. ZO optimization on the other hand only relies on model queries and does not use computational graphs. So ZO optimization can be applied broadly to DL problems with black-box components that can only be queried. Even though ZO optimization is promising, scalability bottlenecks stop it from being used in medium or large-scale DNN training. When the problem dimension increases, traditional ZO methods get worse in accuracy and efficiency. The reason is that ZO gradient estimates based on finite differences are biased estimators of FO gradients, and the bias gets bigger in higher-dimensional spaces.

These challenges lead to the central question of this work: (Q) How to scale up ZO optimization for training deep models? To answer (Q), we propose a new framework, 'DeepZero', which brings in new model pruning and parallel computing techniques to scale up ZO DNN training (see Fig. 1 for an overview). Our main contributions are the following.

- We show that deterministic coordinate-wise gradient estimation (CGE) is better than vector-wise randomized gradient estimation (RGE) in both accuracy and computation efficiency when scaling up to deep model training. Also, CGE gets more and more advantageous as the model depth increases.

- We show that sparsity is crucial to make model training via CGE with finite differences work. Different from prior work, we find that sparsity for black-box models can be obtained for 'free' by extending the current pruning-at-initialization technique to the ZO learning paradigm. This synergy between pruning and CGE is a promising way to train DNNs efficiently with ZO.

- We identify a parallelization-fit property that CGE-based ZO optimization has, and based on it we propose a new forward parallelization method. Our framework allows feature reuse in deep learning, which makes parallel training even faster by removing redundant computations.

- We introduce our ZO deep model training framework, 'DeepZero'. To show that DeepZero is empirically better, we run extensive experiments on standard image classification benchmarks and also on real-world black-box DL applications. For example, when we use DeepZero to train a ResNet20 on CIFAR-10, we get 86.94\% testing accuracy, which is the best reported in the gradient-free model training literature. We also show the large potential and practical impact of DeepZero in two real-world DL tasks: black-box defense for adversarial robustness and physics-informed DL with solver-in-the-loop.

To be clear, our work aims to extend how far ZO optimization scales for DL applications, for the cases where FO optimization is challenging or infeasible. However, the advancements we propose for ZO training are not meant to solve the ultimate scalability challenges of training deep networks at any scale.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In the realm of machine learning (ML), optimization algorithms have played a crucial role in enabling the training of complex models, yielding unprecedented insights and predictive capabilities across diverse domains. Over the years, first-order (FO) gradient-based methods, such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants [1,2,3,4], have become the default choice for model training. These methods rely on gradient information to iteratively update model parameters, aiming to minimize a given loss function. Nonetheless, there are several practical settings where FO gradient information is either unavailable or infeasible to compute, calling for alternative strategies. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization [5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12] has emerged as a promising approach to these challenges, as it uses finite differences of function values to estimate gradients rather than requesting explicit gradient information. Therefore, with minor modifications to FO algorithms, ZO optimization can be applied in various real-world circumstances where FO gradients are difficult to obtain. For example, in disciplines like physics and chemistry, ML models may interact with intricate simulators or experiments whose underlying systems are non-differentiable [13,14,15,16,17]. Additionally, black-box learning scenarios often arise when deep learning (DL) models are integrated with third-party APIs, such as adversarial attack and defense against black-box DL models [18,19,20,21] and black-box prompt learning for language-model-as-a-service [22,23]. Furthermore, the backpropagation (BP) mechanism [2,24] for calculating FO gradients may not be supported when implementing DL models on hardware systems [25,26,27,28,29]. Apart from ZO optimization, another relevant research direction in DL focuses on developing biologically-plausible, BP-free methods, for example forward gradient-based methods [30,31,32,33], greedy layer-wise learning [34], and Hebbian learning [35,36]. However, these techniques require access to computational graphs and are highly dependent on the DL software frameworks and/or model architectures used. In contrast, ZO optimization relies solely on model queries and does not use computational graphs. As a result, ZO optimization is broadly applicable to DL problems that involve black-box, query-only components. Despite its promise, scalability bottlenecks hinder the application of ZO optimization to medium or large-scale DNN training [37,10,38,39,20]. As problem dimensionality increases, the accuracy and efficiency of traditional ZO methods deteriorate, because ZO finite difference-based gradient estimates are biased estimators of FO gradients, and the bias becomes more pronounced in higher-dimensional spaces [10,39,40].

These challenges motivate the central question of this work: (Q) How to scale up ZO optimization for training deep models? To address (Q), we propose a novel framework, 'DeepZero', which combines novel model pruning and parallel computing techniques to scale up ZO DNN training (see Fig. 1 for a schematic overview). Our main contributions are summarized below.

❶ We show that deterministic coordinate-wise gradient estimation (CGE) outperforms vector-wise randomized gradient estimation (RGE) in both accuracy and computation efficiency when scaling to deep model training. Moreover, CGE becomes increasingly advantageous as model depth increases.

❷ We show that sparsity is crucial for realizing model training via CGE with finite differences. In contrast to prior work, we find that sparsity for black-box models can be obtained for 'free' by extending the current pruning-at-initialization technique to the ZO learning paradigm. The synergy between pruning and CGE offers a promising avenue for efficient ZO training of DNNs.

❸ We identify the parallelization-fit property inherent to CGE-based ZO optimization and propose a novel forward parallelization method based on it. Our framework enables feature reuse in deep learning, which further accelerates parallel training by eliminating redundant computations.

❹ We introduce our ZO deep model training framework, 'DeepZero'. To demonstrate its empirical superiority, we conduct extensive experiments on both standard image classification benchmarks and real-world black-box DL applications. For example, when using DeepZero to train a ResNet20 on CIFAR-10, we obtain 86.94\% testing accuracy, the best reported in the literature of gradient-free model training. We also show the vast potential and practical impact of DeepZero in two real-world DL tasks: black-box defense for adversarial robustness [20] and physics-informed DL with solver-in-the-loop [43].

To clarify, our work aims to extend the scalability of ZO optimization for DL applications, addressing cases where FO optimization is challenging or infeasible. Yet it should be noted that the proposed advancements in ZO training are not intended to overcome the ultimate scalability challenges of training deep networks at any scale.
